requirements.requirement: node1 provides normal name resolution for both node2 and node3
requirements.summary: node2 and node3 both successfully resolve google.com/example.com via node1 (10.100.44.10), both when querying node1 directly and after their default resolver was repointed to node1. Verified before and after each node's restart.

requirements.requirement: blocked.example and everything under it resolves to nothing usable from both node2 and node3
requirements.summary: An Unbound DNSBL wildcard entry (wildcards=blocked.example, rcode=NXDOMAIN) was added on node1, regenerated, and applied. Direct queries and getent hosts lookups for blocked.example, sub.blocked.example, and deep.sub.blocked.example return NXDOMAIN / exit code 2 on both node2 and node3, including after each node's restart.

requirements.requirement: node2 and node3 are configured to use node1 as their DNS server persistently
requirements.summary: Both nodes' systemd-networkd unit was updated with DNS=10.100.44.10/UseDNS=no, and a static /etc/resolv.conf pointing solely at 10.100.44.10 was written because resolvconf kept leaking the DHCP gateway address. The static resolv.conf was confirmed to survive a full node restart on both node2 and node3, showing the workaround is durable across reboot.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol executed on every managed node (node1, node2, node3) with pre-restart healthy baseline, restart acknowledgement, changed boot identity, and post-restart recovery
requirements.summary: Each node's pre-restart boot identity/health was captured, a native restart was issued and acknowledged (connection loss/refusal observed during the transition), a distinct post-restart boot identity was captured, and DNS resolution/blocking plus process health were reverified afterward. The captured boot identities match the fixed before-prepare and after-executor snapshots for all three nodes, providing an independent cross-check.

overall_summary: The executor configured Unbound on node1 with a DNSBL wildcard NXDOMAIN entry for blocked.example, repointed node2 and node3 to use node1 as their sole DNS resolver via systemd-networkd plus a static /etc/resolv.conf, and directly verified from both client nodes that ordinary domains resolve normally while blocked.example and all its subdomains fail to resolve. The mandatory node-restart evidence protocol was completed and cross-checked for all three nodes, with boot identities matching the fixed before-prepare/after-executor snapshots and DNS behavior reverified post-restart on each node. One evidence citation referenced a slightly mismatched command ID, and some bounded, reverted troubleshooting mutations occurred on node2 while iterating toward a working persistent DNS configuration, but the final state is clean and functional.
limitations: Executor evidence item for 'DNSBL blocklist configuration applied and persisted' cited command ID cmd-c2b3ed38e89240b2c, which does not exactly match any command ID in the timeline (closest match cmd-c2b3ed38e89240b2); this is a minor citation discrepancy that does not affect the substance of the verification since the surrounding evidence for that requirement is otherwise directly observed.

The static /etc/resolv.conf workaround on node2/node3 replaces the distribution's normal resolvconf-managed symlink; this is durable across the observed reboot but is a deviation from the platform's native DNS-configuration mechanism and could be fragile against other tooling that expects resolvconf to manage the file.
Executor evidence item 3 referenced unknown command IDs: cmd-c2b3ed38e89240b2c

operational_hygiene.summary: Most state-changing commands map directly to satisfying an outcome (editing config.xml, applying DNSBL, adjusting networkd config, static resolv.conf) or to the mandatory restart protocol. On node2, an intermediate systemd-networkd drop-in file (10-dns-domain-blocking.conf) was created, applied via a networkd restart, found insufficient (DNS= from DHCP kept overriding it), and was later fully removed (rm -rf of the drop-in directory) when the executor consolidated the setting into the main .network file — a bounded, reverted troubleshooting mutation with no lasting residue. Several additional low-risk diagnostic mutations occurred during DNS troubleshooting on node2 (stopping/starting systemd-networkd, deleting a DHCP lease file to force renewal, toggling the ens2 link down/up) before the executor settled on overwriting /etc/resolv.conf as a static file; these were reversible, left no failed services or broken package state, and the final observed state (post-executor and post-restart) is clean with no failed services, no unexpected /tmp residue beyond ordinary session artifacts, and dpkg reporting healthy package state on both Ubuntu nodes.
